lede: Vessantara / Mahāchat accounts for 85 catalogued manuscripts, 3 of them flagged research-priority. It clusters in Lampang (49% of the corpus for this subject), ahead of Phrae and Nan. Nearly all (99%) are written in Tham Lanna · อักษรธรรมล้านนา script. By support it leans to palm-leaf · ใบลาน (94%) over mulberry paper (saa) · กระดาษสา (6%). Dated witnesses run 1646–1951 CE (69 of 85 carry a date).

authored.title: Vessantara / Mahāchat
authored.body_html:
What this is

The Vessantara — the Mahāchat, มหาชาติ, "the Great Birth" — is the last of the ten final lives of the Buddha-to-be, and the most copied story in this archive. It is the story of a prince who gives away everything, in the wrong order, to the wrong people, and is right to. Lanna did not merely preserve it. Lanna recited it once a year in a marathon that took a full day, split it into thirteen sponsorable chapters so that thirteen families could each own one, wrote out at least sixty-nine named performance versions of it, and then carried its syllables into the magical curriculum, where the whole birth-tale is compressed to four letters you can chant over your own flesh.

This page tells the story first, because the catalogue makes no sense without it.

The story, first

Tradition holds — it opens with a white elephant that makes rain. Prince Vessantara of Sivi is born with his hand out — his first words, the tradition says, are a request for something to give away — and grows up practising dāna, generosity, as an athlete practises a lift. His kingdom owns a white elephant that brings the monsoon. A delegation arrives from a neighbouring kingdom in drought and asks for it. He gives it to them.

The city riots. An elephant that makes rain is not a possession, it is the state's water supply, and the prince has handed it to foreigners because they asked politely. The citizens force the king to exile him. Vessantara accepts, asks for one day to complete the Gift of the Seven Hundreds — seven hundred each of elephants, horses, chariots, women, cattle, slaves, and vessels of wine — empties the treasury, and leaves in a carriage with his wife Maddī and their two small children, Jāli and Kaṇhā. On the road brahmins ask for the horses; he gives them. One asks for the carriage; he gives it. The family walks the rest of the way into the Himavanta forest and builds two leaf huts.

Then the story does the thing that has kept people arguing about it for two thousand years. An old brahmin named Jūjaka — grasping, ugly, and married to a young wife who is tired of drawing her own water — walks into the forest to ask for the children as slaves. He times it for a day when Maddī is out gathering fruit, because he knows the mother will not allow it. Vessantara gives away Jāli and Kaṇhā. The children hide in a lotus pond; their father calls them out; Jūjaka beats them in front of him and drives them off tied at the wrists, and Vessantara sits with his hand on his sword and does not move, because the perfection he is completing is the perfection of not taking back. Maddī comes home at dusk to an empty hut and searches the forest all night before he tells her. The next morning a disguised Indra arrives and asks for Maddī. He gives her too — and Indra immediately gives her back, which is the story admitting that this last gift was a test and the previous one was not.

Tradition holds — it ends in reunion and it is not a comfortable one. Jūjaka, steering by greed, blunders into the very city the children were born in; their grandfather recognises them and ransoms them at the extravagant price Jāli had set on his own head; Jūjaka eats himself to death at the celebration feast. The exile is lifted, the six royals meet in the forest and faint together — the chapter called Chakkhattiya, "the six nobles" — and the family goes home. But nobody in the audience has forgotten the pond, and the recitation does not ask them to. The point of the Great Birth is not that generosity feels good. It is that the last perfection before Buddhahood costs more than a listener would pay.

Inference — that discomfort is exactly why it became the communal text rather than a private one. A story this hard is not read alone; it is performed, out loud, in a building full of people, once a year, with the hardest chapters sponsored by name.

What the catalogue holds

Eighty-five manuscripts carry Wetsantala in the title. Their shape is canonical and old: 80 of 85 palm-leaf, 84 of 85 Tham Lanna, 69 of them dated, running 1646 to 1951. Seventy-six sit under jātaka; the rest scatter into Buddhist canonical (4), magic & ritual (3), poetry (1) and liturgy (1). Geographically it does not behave like plain jātaka, which piles up in the great scriptorium at Wat Sung Men: here Lampang leads with 42 against Phrae's 25, and within Lampang a single village temple, Wat Ban Luk, holds 24 copies on its own.

But 85 badly undercounts it, and the reason is instructive. Lanna scribes usually did not write "Vessantara" on the bundle. They wrote the chapter names. A typical Wat Sung Men title runs: Tatsapon, Himmapan, Tanakhan, Wannapawet, Cucok, Cunlapon, Mahapon, Sakkaban, Mahalat, Sakkati, Nakon — eleven of the thirteen chapters listed in order, with no work-title at all, because everyone knew. Count manuscripts whose titles either name Vessantara or list two or more chapters of his cycle and the figure rises to 182, of which 172 are filed as jātaka — roughly one in nine of the 1,633-manuscript jātaka shelf. On that count the province order flips back: Phrae 76, Lampang 67, Nan 18, with 58 at Wat Sung Men alone. One diagnostic name alone does most of the work: 74 manuscripts name ชูชก Jūjaka in the title. The beggar who takes the children is, by title-frequency, the most famous character in Lanna's manuscript literature.

Thirteen chapters, thirteen books

The thirteen kan — ทศพร Thatsaphon (the ten boons), หิมพานต์ Himaphan (the Himavanta forest), ทานกัณฑ์ Thanakhan (the great giving), วนประเวศน์ Wannapawet (entering the wood), ชูชก Jūjaka, จุลพน Cunlaphon (the lesser forest), มหาพน Mahāphon (the greater forest), กุมาร Kumān (the children), มัทรี Maddī, สักกบรรพ Sakkabap (Indra's chapter), มหาราช Mahārāt (the great king), ฉกษัตริย์ Chakkhattiya (the six nobles), นครกัณฑ์ Nakhon (the return to the city) — are not just an internal division. In this catalogue they are physically separate objects. Beyond the composite bundles, the catalogue holds witnesses whose titles name one chapter and nothing else: ชูชก Cucok, ms 4048, Wat Bun Yuen in Nan, 1884, eight leaves; มัทธี Matthi, ms 4791, Wat Chedi Luang in Chiang Mai, six leaves; มหาพล Mahapon, ms 5119, Wat Wiang in Lampang, 1759, five leaves; มหาราช Mahalat twice over at Wat Lai Hin Luang in Lampang, one of them dated 1722. Five leaves is not a book. It is a part. Inference — that is what a sponsorship economy leaves behind in a library. If your family's obligation at the festival is the Maddī chapter, what you commission, own, lend and store is the Maddī chapter, and the great composite bundles are the temple's master copies rather than the working ones.

The order in the titles is not always the printed order, either. Ms 5008 at Wat Ban Ueam (Lampang, 1872) lists Cucok, Mahapon, Culapon — the two forest chapters transposed. Ms 5006 (1860, same temple) drops Jūjaka's chapter entirely and keeps the rest. Inference — these are performance sets, and a set is missing a chapter because that year somebody else had it.

Sixty-nine editions with names

The single most striking thing in the Vessantara data is a habit of the Lanna colophon: the bundle ends with ฉบับ + a name, "the version of ___." Of the 182 Vessantara-cycle manuscripts, 83 carry such a tag, and they use 69 distinct names between them. These are not edition numbers. They are groves, villages, persons and jokes:

  • ฉบับเถ้าลืมตื่น sabap thao luem tuen — "the old man who forgot to wake" (ms 1666, Wat Sung Men, 1877)
  • ฉบับวิงวอน sabap wing won, "entreaty" — with a whole family around it: ฉบับวิงวอนดอนแก้ว (ms 5006, Wat Ban Ueam, Lampang, 1860), ฉบับวิงวอนดอนกลาง (ms 5312, Wat Ban Luk, Lampang, 1787), ฉบับวิงวอนดอนกางเชียงใหม่ (ms 1751, Wat Sung Men, 1801), and the splendid ฉบับวิงวอนมวนอาระขะเก้าหน้า (ms 2663, Wat Phra Luang, Phrae)
  • the forest versions — ฉบับป่ากล้วย "banana grove" (ms 2731, Wat Mueang Mo, 1910), ฉบับป่าไผ่ "bamboo grove" (ms 3644, Wat Kittiwong, Mae Hong Son), ฉบับป่าเหียง (ms 2712, 1872), ฉบับป่าฝาง (ms 2718, 1840), ฉบับป่าชาง (ms 4856, Wat Phra That Lampang Luang, 1805), ฉบับแม่กุป่าหลิน (ms 5358, Wat Ban Luk, 1791)
  • ฉบับพันนาเชียงรุ้ง — Phanna Chiang Rung, which is to say Sipsongpanna, the Lue country up the Mekong. Eight manuscripts carry it, spelled four different ways (พันนาเชียงรุ่ง, พันนาเชียงรุ้ง, พันนาเชียรุ้ง, พันนาเชืยงรุ้ง), from 1839 to 1909, at Wat Sung Men and Wat Mueang Mo in Phrae and Wat Hang Chat and Wat Ban Ueam in Lampang. Inference — a foreign house-version that four scribal communities all thought worth naming, and none of them agreed how to spell.
  • ฉบับพระยอดส้อยเมืองคลางเชียงไหม and ฉบับพระสิงหลวงเมืองเชืยงไหม่ — two Chiang Mai versions, copied out at Wat Ban Ueam in Lampang (ms 5008, 1872) and Wat Klang in Phrae (ms 2812, 1916), neither of them anywhere near Chiang Mai
  • ฉบับโสฬสสิบหกเมือง — "the sixteen mueang," twice over in one phrase, Pali and Thai (ms 1793, Wat Sung Men, 1913)
  • ฉบับตลุง และทะโค่ง — a Himaphan chapter tagged with two recension names at once, with the Cucok in the same bundle tagged with the second of them alone (ms 622, Wat Na Pang, Nan, 1888)
  • ฉบับลวงฅำ sabap luang kham, the most travelled: Wat Sung Men in 1870 and again in 1890, Wat Don Chai Phra Bat in Nan in 1891, Wat Mueang Mo in 1905 — one named version crossing two provinces over thirty-five years

Inference — a text does not accumulate sixty-nine named versions by being read. It accumulates them by being performed — these are the recitation styles, melodies and house-texts of a competitive annual event, and the ฉบับ tag is the scribe recording which one this copy sings. This is the single richest untapped index in the catalogue: a ฉบับ facet would let a reader trace one house-version across temples and decades, which is a question no title search can currently ask.

The apparatus for putting it on

The Vessantara does not travel alone. Around the birth-story the catalogue holds the whole working kit of the Thet Mahachat festival, and each piece belongs to a different genre — which is why this entity is the archive's best demonstration that the genre walls are porous.

The invitation. Kam alathana tham wetsantala, คำอาราธนาธัมม์เวสสันตระ — the ārādhanā words that formally invite a monk to preach the Great Birth. There are four in the catalogue and, tellingly, all four come from Nan: ms 314 and ms 370 from Wat Si Mongkhon (Kong) — the same formula catalogued once as magic & ritual and once as liturgy, a filing disagreement that is itself the argument of this page — and ms 492 and ms 516 from Wat Pa Mueat. Look at what ms 516 is bound with: the Vessantara invitation, the words for calling the khwan, and a sut thon, all in one bundle. A fifth ārādhanā manuscript from the same district, ms 416 at Wat Hia, binds a different invitation — the one for the Rains Retreat — in beside a suep cata life-extension procedure. Inference — these are not scripture volumes. They are an officiant's working folder: the four or five things a village ritual specialist actually gets asked to do.

The merit-accounting. Anisong wetsantala, อานิสงส์เวสสันตระ — the ānisaṃsa that enumerates what a listener earns by hearing the whole recitation in a single day. Twenty-five witnesses name it. Some stand alone — ms 5439 at Wat Ban Luk (Lampang, 1782), ms 3832 at Wat Si Khom Kham (Phayao, 1860), ms 1252 at Wat Kittiwong (Mae Hong Son, 1704) — but most sit at the end of a full thirteen-chapter bundle, after Nakhon kan, exactly where a reckoning of the day's merit belongs when the day is over.

The thousand verses. ms 2714 at Wat Mueang Mo (Phrae, 1905) closes its bundle with สหัสสะคาถามหาเวสสันตระ, the Sahassa-gāthā — the "thousand verses," the Pali skeleton of the whole tale that a preacher chants through as the spine of the performance. The printed biography of Luang Por Thob (p.6) confirms it was still a working skill in the twentieth century. Having taken the full transmission of incantation-lore from his two teachers, the young Luang Por Thob went on to "practise chanting the Mahachat sermon, in both the คาถาพัน verse-formulas and the กัณฑ์ราย sermon-chapters, in the style favoured by people of that era, most beautifully" — the same two-part technique the Phrae manuscript preserves, listed by a Central Thai devotional biography as one of a famous magician-monk's accomplishments, alongside the katha.

The night before. Bundles again and again put มาลัยหมื่น มาลัยแสน, the Malai texts, immediately before the Vessantara chapters — ms 1639 at Wat Sung Men (1811) lists Malai muen malai saen right after Nakhon; ms 1749 and ms 2710 sandwich Pathama malai and Tutiya malai between the last chapter and the anisong. Tradition holds — Phra Malai's tour of the hells and the heavens is recited on the eve of Thet Mahachat, and it is Malai who brings back Metteyya's condition for meeting him: hear the entire Vessantara in one day. Inference — the binding order in these bundles is the running order of the festival.

The version for fun. ms 556, คำเหล้นคร่าวเวสสันตระ Kam len khao wetsantala, from Wat Bun Yuen in Nan — the khao, a Lanna verse form, "words for playing the Vessantara." Filed under poetry, because that is what it is. The same story that earns a listener a shot at the next Buddha is also the one you set to a tune and enjoy.

And the version filed as history. ms 3451, ตำนานเวสสันตระ Tamnan wetsantala, Wat Kasa, Chiang Rai, 1930 — a scribe who reached for tamnan, the word for a chronicle, and used it for a birth-tale. (The cataloguer put it back on the jātaka shelf.) Five registers, then, not four: scripture, liturgical cue, merit-manual, folk-song, and — for at least one copyist in Chiang Rai — history.

Vessantara inside the wichaa

Where the Great Birth gets genuinely strange is on the magical shelf, where the whole thirteen-chapter epic is treated as a power with a heart-syllable, like a god or a weapon.

Two separate printed treatises, from different lineages, carry the same curriculum table: a column of syllables against a column of what they compress. In the Vedic katha for chai chatri (p.51) it reads สะระตะนะ — พระเวสสันดร; in the Khom-Thai inscription formulas (p.21) it reads สะระนะตะ — หัวใจพระเวสสันดร, "the heart of Vessantara," two letters transposed by one copyist or the other. In both books the neighbourhood is the same — the Boiling Ganges sits directly above it — and in the fuller of the two the rest of the final lives run on down the column: Vidhura, Mahosadha, Temiya, Bhūridatta the naga-prince, Suvaṇṇasāma, Mahājanaka. Ten whole birth-tales as a set of four-syllable keys, each a jātaka folded into a chant. Inference — on this shelf a birth-tale is not a text you read. It is a battery.

The Compendium of Ancient Katha shows what that looks like at full length. Its Great Assembly invocation — the one whose closing note reads "this katha, the great assembly of devas, is said before performing any working at all" — runs on for pages, summoning everything there is: the future Buddha Metteyya, Kaccāyana, Aṅgulimāla, Ānanda, the seven planets and Rāhu, Shiva and Vishnu, the sixteen Brahma heavens by name, the rivers, the monkey army of the Rāmāyaṇa — and, in the middle of it, the Ten Births one by one, arriving at "Phra Vessantara and Queen Maddī, the children Kaṇhā and Jāli, the Great Bodhi Tree, and the excellent heart born of generosity." The family is invoked as a unit, children included, as though they were a deity with a retinue.

And then the best sentence about the Great Birth in the entire corpus, from the same book (p.25). The คาถาปลุกเครื่อง, the katha for awakening the body and its equipment, walks down the practitioner's own anatomy converting each part into armour: hair to diamond fur, twenty nails to bronze, thirty-two teeth to magic iron, skin to an amulet-vest, nine hundred great tendons to jewelled cloth, bones to kapok — and, in the middle of the list:

"มังสัง — my flesh, all three hundred pieces, becomes the Great Birth Tale (มหาชาติ), granting invulnerability."

Inference — nothing else in the archive states the Vessantara's standing so economically. Every other item on that list is a substance — metal, stone, cloth, fibre. In the flesh slot, where you would expect iron, the treatise puts a story. The Great Birth is what the practitioner's body is made of.

Two smaller sightings complete the set. The Phetcharat great yantra manual (p.76) prints a square yant with a diamond inscribed inside and four corner cells of Khom, and glosses it: "This Phra Kala image is Phra Vessantara" — the prince as the identity of a yantra, with instructions to consecrate it "so that the mouth becomes a charm of attraction." Inference — a figure whose defining act is giving without limit makes obvious sense as a persuasion-charm: what he is famous for is being unable to say no.

Jūjaka goes to market

The strangest afterlife belongs to the villain. On the archive's market layer — the 13,020-listing Lazada snapshot — eight listings name ชูชก Jūjaka, and none of them treats him as a cautionary tale. He is a wealth charm. There is a เหรียญโภคทรัพย์ prosperity coin with Nang Kwak the beckoning lady on the front and Jūjaka on the reverse, listed as หลวงปู่อั๊บ, วัดท้องไทร, Nakhon Pathom, 2552 BE. There is a second Nang Kwak coin "backed with Grandfather Jūjaka, the Great Fortune, Great Millionaire edition." There is a cast figure of him attributed to หลวงปู่ทิม at ฿500. There are two hun payont effigies of Jūjaka in lek lai metal at ฿90 each. There is a silver piece packed with the prai powder of fifty-nine spirits, showing Jūjaka paired with นางอมิตดา, his young wife, at ฿5,500. And there is น้ำมันชูชก, "Jūjaka oil," sold under the frank subtitle น้ำมันขอเมีย — "the oil for asking for a wife" — at ฿550.

Inference — the market has read the story with total accuracy and no sentiment whatsoever. Jūjaka is the man in the tale who asks for the impossible and gets it, and who ends up with a young wife he did nothing to deserve. Strip the morality out and that is a functional specification. The Great Birth's whole moral architecture depends on Vessantara being the one you admire — and the amulet trade, needing a patron of successful asking, went straight past him to the brahmin at the door.

Notes

  • Numbers on this page, and what they count. 85 is manuscripts with Wetsantala in the title; 182 is manuscripts naming Vessantara or listing two or more chapters of his cycle; 74 name Jūjaka; 69 is distinct ฉบับ recension names; 25 carry an anisong; 4 carry the Vessantara ārādhanā invitation. The 85-set's profile (76 jātaka, 80 palm-leaf, 1646–1951, Lampang 42 / Phrae 25) was checked against the catalogue and stands as previously published.
  • ฉบับ is the facet this archive is missing. Sixty-nine named versions across 83 manuscripts is a performance tradition hiding inside a metadata field. Inference — extracting ฉบับ into a browsable facet would be a small parse over existing titles and would open a question — which house-version travelled where — that nothing on the site can currently answer. It is the highest-value cheap index in the catalogue.
  • Chapter-level indexing is now demonstrably worth it. Because the thirteen kan have stable names and appear as standalone witnesses, a Jūjaka facet or a Maddī facet is buildable from titles alone, and would surface dozens of manuscripts that the current entity search does not connect to this page at all.
  • Read it beside the rite pages. The su khwan, sut thon and suep cata entities share physical bundles with the Vessantara invitation in Nan; the katha and yantra pages hold the forms its heart-syllable is filed under; and the naga page follows Bhūridatta, who stands four names away from Vessantara in the same invocation and, like him, is famous for refusing to take anything back.
